name: Cabo Verde
summary_text: Cabo Verde does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Article 71 of the 1886 Penal Code had prohibited unnatural acts. A 2004 amendment removed all provisions on consensual homosexual sex.  No legal gender recognition framework is on record. Civil law blocked a change to a female legal name sought by Tchinda Andrade, the first publicly self-outed transgender woman in Cabo Verde who came out in 1997 at age 19 and in a local newspaper in 1998. The inventory holds no later statute or administrative procedure permitting a legal gender change. A visitor whose passport marker differs from presentation should expect no local precedent for documentary flexibility.  Workplace protection does not cover gender identity. Articles 45(2) and 406(3) of the Labour Code have prohibited employment discrimination based on sexual orientation since 2008. A transgender worker therefore has no explicit statutory basis for a workplace complaint on gender identity grounds.  Cabo Verde does not recognise same-sex unions. Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva said on 11 July 2017 that same-sex marriage was not on the government agenda. He distanced himself from opposition expressed by MpD secretary-general Miguel Monteiro after community demands for civil unions and marriage.  Societal discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity was found to continue as a problem in the 2010 United States Department of State human rights report, despite legal provisions protecting homosexual conduct. In a 22 June 2016 interview, Andrade reported verbal violence and two physical attacks, while describing Cabo Verde as markedly free for LGBT people in comparison with other countries on the continent.  Official signals are protective at international level and engaged domestically. Cabo Verde signed United Nations documents in 2008 stating human rights are not limited by sexual orientation or gender identity and in 2011 condemning violence and discrimination against LGBT people. It is one of two African members of the UN LGBTI Core Group, made anti-discrimination commitments in the 2024 Universal Periodic Review, and in 2025 signed a Spain-proposed joint declaration for LGBTQ rights as the only African signatory. LGBTIQ organisations register freely. The state gender-equality institute ICIEG engaged with Pride organising alongside UN Women, which indicates institutional contact points a visitor could approach.

sources.documents: Trans-specific living conditions: most popular transgender person/activist Tchinda Andrade came out in local newspaper in 1998; described by CNN as 'mother hen'; locals refer to transgender people as 'tchindas'; documentary following São Vicente Carnival preparations won Grand Jury Award at Outfest and Africa Movie Academy Award nomination.

name: Cuba
summary_text: Private, non-commercial sexual relations between consenting same-sex adults aged 16 and over have been lawful in Cuba since 1979, when the Social Defence Code that treated homosexual practices as a social threat was repealed. The offence of public display of homosexual condition was repealed in 1987. The offence of bothering or soliciting with homosexual requests was amended in 1997 to refer only to sexual requests.  Article 42 of the 2019 Constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. It was the first constitutional text to name both grounds expressly. The definition of marriage as between a man and a woman in Article 36 was removed in the February 2019 referendum, with marriage defined on the basis of free will and equality of rights.  Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation is unlawful in Cuba. Discrimination on the basis of gender identity is also unlawful. In employment, Law 116 and the labour amendment approved in December 2013 bar discrimination on sexual orientation. Article 2(b) of the Labour Code covers orientation and does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground.  Following the Family Code referendum on 25 September 2022, Cuba recognises same-sex marriage and unions, same-sex adoption and non-commercial surrogacy. The referendum proposal also included codified domestic-violence penalties and shared parental rights. The Code confirms that legal gender change does not require surgery.  Transgender health care is provided within the public health system under Resolution 126 of 2008.  Police received orders in 1988 not to harass lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons after repeal of the 1938 Public Ostentation Law. In 2001 police prevented gay and trans persons from meeting in the street, fined them and closed meeting places. In 2004 police conducted a campaign directed at travestis and arrested persons dressed in women's clothing.  Since 1993 lesbian, gay and bisexual persons and transgender persons may serve openly in the Cuban Revolutionary Armed Forces.  Pride parades are held in Havana every May to coincide with the International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia, with attendance growing each year. Cuba voted in 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2025 in favour of renewing the mandate of the United Nations independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity.

sources.title: Penal Code of Cuba (1979) - repeal of Social Defence Code
sources.documents: Decriminalization of private, adult, non-commercial consensual same-sex relations age 16+; repealed Code that called 'homosexual practices' a 'social threat'.
sources.detail: Article text: 'The Social Defence Code, which characterized "homosexual practices" as a "social threat"... was repealed in 1979 by the Penal Code of Cuba. This Code did not criminalize homosexuality per se.' No URL visible in text.
